body.text: This page explains the latest IRS guidance on R&D tax credit refund claims for U.S. taxpayers filing Section 41 claims on amended returns. Valid claims must identify all business components, the research activities for each, and total qualified wage, supply, and contract research expenses, with the 45-day perfection period currently running through January 10, 2027.

Status date: November 11, 2026. Scope: what the IRS currently requires for a Section 41 research credit claim for refund to be valid, and the Form 6765 and examination rules that apply to those claims.
1. Summary

items: The IRS's specificity requirements for research credit refund claims under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 date from IRS News Release IR-2021-203 (issued October 15, 2021), which announced Office of Chief Counsel Field Attorney Advice memorandum FAA 20214101F. That memorandum constitutes internal legal advice to IRS examination and processing staff regarding the application of Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1); under IRC § 6110(k)(3), it is not a statute or a legislative regulation and may not be used or cited as binding legal precedent.

Under Research Credit Claims (Section 41) on Amended Returns Frequently Asked Questions (FAQ) 21 (added June 18, 2024), a research credit claim for refund postmarked as of June 18, 2024, no longer has to provide the names of the individuals who performed each research activity or state the specific information each individual sought to discover at the time the refund claim is filed. However, the IRS explicitly retains the authority to request both categories of individual-level substantiation if the refund claim is selected for examination.

To satisfy the administrative specificity threshold under Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1), a valid Section 41 refund claim must still: (1) identify all business components to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that tax year; (2) for each business component, identify all research activities performed; and (3) provide the total qualified employee wage expenses, total qualified supply expenses, and total qualified contract research expenses for the claim year. This third requirement may be satisfied by properly completing and attaching Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities.

The administrative transition period, which grants taxpayers a 45-day window to perfect a deficient research credit claim for refund prior to a final IRS determination of disallowance or rejection, currently runs through January 10, 2027, pursuant to IRS News Release IR-2025-99 (issued October 1, 2025) and Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) procedural update ts-21-0126-0032 (dated January 2, 2026). None of the authoritative IRS sources consulted as of November 11, 2026, reflects a further extension beyond January 10, 2027.

Section G (Business Component Information) of the redesigned Form 6765 (Rev. December 2024 / Instructions Rev. December 2025) remains optional for all filers for tax years beginning before January 1, 2026 (including the 2025 tax year), and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 (beginning with the 2026 tax year). Crucially for refund claim practice, the small-taxpayer exemption from completing Section G—applicable to taxpayers with qualified research expenses (QREs) of $1.5 million or less and gross receipts of $50 million or less, determined at the controlled group level—applies strictly when the research credit is claimed on a timely filed original return. Under the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765, taxpayers filing amended-return refund claims do not qualify for the small-taxpayer original-return exemption, and must also complete Column 49(f) detailing the information sought to be discovered for each business component.

body.text: 2. Origin of the Refund-Claim Requirements
2.1 IR-2021-203 and Chief Counsel Memorandum 20214101F

On October 15, 2021, the Internal Revenue Service issued News Release IR-2021-203 concurrently with Office of Chief Counsel Field Attorney Advice memorandum FAA 20214101F (dated September 17, 2021, and publicly released October 15, 2021). The memorandum establishes the minimum factual elements that a taxpayer's IRC § 41 research credit claim for refund must contain when filed on an amended return (such as Form 1120-X, Form 1040-X, or an Administrative Adjustment Request under IRC § 6227) in order to be treated as a valid claim for administrative processing and for purposes of conferring federal court jurisdiction under IRC § 7422(a). Its stated legal foundation is the longstanding specificity requirement codified in Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1), which mandates that a claim for credit or refund must set forth in detail each ground upon which a credit or refund is claimed and facts sufficient to apprise the Commissioner of the exact basis thereof, verified by a written declaration made under the penalties of perjury.

In IR-2021-203 and FAA 20214101F, the IRS enumerated five specific elements—subsequently referred to across IRS administrative guidance and Internal Revenue Manual provisions as the "five items of information"—that taxpayers were required to submit contemporaneously with the filing of any research credit refund claim:

items: Identify all the business components (as defined in IRC § 41(d)(2)(B)) to which the Section 41 research credit claim relates for that tax year;
For each business component, identify all research activities performed;
Identify all individuals (by name or title) who performed each research activity for each business component;
Describe all the information that each individual sought to discover for each business component; and

Provide the total qualified employee wage expenses (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(i)), total qualified supply expenses (IRC § 41(b)(2)(A)(ii)), and total qualified contract research expenses (IRC § 41(b)(3)) for the claim year (which may be done using Form 6765, Credit for Increasing Research Activities).

body.text: When initially promulgated on October 15, 2021, IR-2021-203 established a grace period running through January 10, 2022, before the new specificity standards took effect, followed by a one-year transition period during which taxpayers whose claims were deemed deficient would be issued a notice and granted 30 days to perfect the refund claim. On January 5, 2022, the IRS updated its administrative procedures via the Research Credit Claims FAQs to expand the perfection window from 30 days to 45 days.

In fact, IR-2021-203 is the public IRS News Release issued on October 15, 2021, whereas the underlying legal memorandum authored by the Office of Chief Counsel is Field Attorney Advice (FAA) 20214101F.

Legal weight: Pursuant to IRC § 6110(k)(3), a Chief Counsel advice memorandum or Field Attorney Advice constitutes a written determination issued to internal IRS personnel and may not be used or cited as precedent. The binding legal obligation governing refund claim validity derives directly from IRC § 7422(a) and Treasury Regulation § 301.6402-2(b)(1), as interpreted by federal courts under the anti-surprise and administrative screening doctrines. Memorandum 20214101F, the IRS Research Credit Claims FAQs, and News Releases IR-2021-203 and IR-2025-99 represent administrative guidance and processing instructions detailing how the IRS evaluates compliance with Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) at the intake and screening stage.
2.2 Judicial Background: Siemer Milling

The verified judicial holding in Siemer Milling is more specific: the United States Tax Court sustained the Commissioner's disallowance of the taxpayer's claimed IRC § 41 research credits across seven alleged projects for the fiscal tax years ended May 31, 2011, and May 31, 2012, because the taxpayer failed to carry its evidentiary burden of proving that its activities constituted "qualified research" within the meaning of IRC § 41(d). Specifically, for every project at issue, the taxpayer failed to establish a methodical process of experimentation, and for several projects, failed to establish the specific business component it sought to develop or improve or failed to demonstrate true technological uncertainty.

While "permitted purpose" (evaluating whether the research is intended for a new or improved function, performance, reliability, or quality under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A)) is a common practitioner shorthand for an element of the business component test, the Tax Court in Siemer Milling Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2019-37, and in subsequent opinions such as Kapur v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-28, formally enumerates the four statutory tests under IRC § 41(d)(1) and (d)(2)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b) as: (1) the Section 174 test (requiring that expenditures qualify as research or experimental expenditures under IRC § 174, or IRC § 174A for post-2024 domestic expenditures); (2) the technological information test (requiring that research be undertaken for the purpose of discovering information that is technological in nature); (3) the business component test (requiring that the taxpayer intend to apply the discovered information in the development of a new or improved business component held for sale, lease, or license, or used in the taxpayer's trade or business); and (4) the process of experimentation test (requiring that substantially all of the research activities constitute elements of a process of experimentation relating to a qualified purpose). Under IRC § 41(d)(2)(A), these four tests must be applied separately to each business component of the taxpayer.
3. The June 18, 2024 Waiver (FAQ 21)

On June 18, 2024, following extensive practitioner feedback regarding the administrative burden of compiling employee-by-employee narratives at the initial refund filing stage, the IRS added FAQ 21 to its webpage titled Research credit claims (Section 41) on amended returns frequently asked questions. Under FAQ 21, the IRS announced that it waives two of the original five items of information required by FAA 20214101F: specifically, Item 3 (the names of the individuals who performed each research activity) and Item 4 (the information each individual sought to discover). This administrative waiver applies strictly to the threshold documentation that must be submitted with the amended return or refund claim at the time of filing to pass initial validity screening. The IRS explicitly cautions in FAQ 21 that both waived items may still be requested and required for substantiation if a research credit refund claim is selected for examination.

Conflict in IRS wording: There is a minor textual discrepancy across official IRS publications regarding the exact effective date of the FAQ 21 waiver on June 18, 2024. The June 18, 2024 update to the IR-2021-203 news release page and the text of FAQ 21 itself state that the waiver applies to refund claims postmarked "as of June 18, 2024." Conversely, the November 25, 2024 administrative update and News Release IR-2025-99 (issued October 1, 2025) describe the streamlined three-item validity requirements as governing claims postmarked "after June 18, 2024." However, Internal Revenue Manual (IRM) procedural update ts-21-0126-0032 (issued January 2, 2026), which directs IRS service center screening personnel on claim processing, instructs examiners to apply the waived standard to claims dated "June 18, 2024 and later."
3.1 What a Valid Claim Must Contain Now

cells: Identify all business components the claim relates to for that year
Yes
Identify all research activities performed for each business component
Yes
Total qualified employee wage, supply, and contract research expenses for the claim year (Form 6765 may be used)
Yes
Names of individuals who performed each research activity
No; waived at filing, but may be requested on examination
Information each individual sought to discover
No; waived at filing, but may be requested on examination

body.text: Two additional procedural rules established in the IRS Research Credit Claims FAQs govern the submission of these items. First, the specificity requirements apply equally to both formal refund claims and informal refund claims. Second, pursuant to FAQ 17 (updated October 30, 2023) and Chief Counsel guidance, corporate taxpayers that file Form 1120 cannot rely on an informal claim for refund for the Section 41 research credit submitted during an ongoing examination if the claim is submitted after the statute of limitations for filing a refund claim has expired, and must instead file a formal amended return (Form 1120-X) satisfying the refund claim validity rules within the statutory limitations period under IRC § 6511.

Note on a conflicting IRS page: Because the dedicated IRS Research Credit Claims FAQ page (last reviewed October 1, 2026), News Release IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), and IRM procedural update ts-21-0126-0032 (January 2, 2026) represent more specific, authoritative, and recently promulgated statements of active IRS administration, this report relies on them over the unrevised summary webpage.
4. The Transition (Perfection) Period

During the administrative transition period, if the IRS determines during initial screening that a timely filed research credit refund claim fails to provide the required items of information, the IRS does not immediately reject the claim as deficient. Instead, the IRS sends the taxpayer a written deficiency notice—specifically Letter 6426C or Letter 6428—that identifies which required information is missing and grants the taxpayer 45 days from the date of the letter to perfect the claim by submitting the missing details before the IRS makes a final determination on the claim (FAQ 7). If the taxpayer timely submits the missing information within the 45-day perfection window, the claim is treated as filed on its original submission date for purposes of the IRC § 6511 statute of limitations.

body.text: Consequently, the expiration date that IR-2025-99 superseded was January 10, 2026, not January 10, 2025. Under IR-2021-203, the original one-year transition period commenced on January 10, 2022, and was scheduled to expire on January 10, 2023; January 10, 2025, represented the expiration date following the second annual extension (issued October 30, 2023). The current January 10, 2027 expiration date is verified across IR-2025-99, the introductory banner of the IRS Research Credit Claims FAQ page, and IRM procedural update ts-21-0126-0032 (January 2, 2026).

Analysis: As of the status date of this report (November 11, 2026), the current transition period is scheduled to expire in exactly 60 days (less than two months). None of the authoritative IRS releases or Internal Revenue Manual updates consulted reflects a further extension beyond January 10, 2027. Unless the IRS issues a fifth extension prior to January 10, 2027, research credit refund claims postmarked after that date that omit any of the three mandatory items of information (or required Form 6765 disclosures) risk summary rejection as invalid claims without a 45-day cure letter under Letter 6426C or Letter 6428—potentially barring recovery permanently if the IRC § 6511 statute of limitations expires in the interim. Taxpayers and practitioners should therefore treat every amended-return refund claim as requiring complete, perfected business-component and QRE documentation upon initial filing.
5. Form 6765 Changes That Affect Refund Claims
5.1 Revision History and Comment Period

items: The IRS published an initial preview draft of the redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) on September 15, 2023, proposing new sections—including what is now Section G—to standardize business-component-level reporting on the face of the tax return. IR-2025-99 also references draft instructions announced in a December 20, 2024 news release (IR-2024-315).

Following stakeholder feedback, the IRS released the updated Form 6765 bearing the revision date "Rev. December 2024" (publicly posted in early 2025, with tax commentary noting final form availability in February 2025), while the accompanying draft instructions released in January 2025 referred to the "January 2025 revision of Form 6765."

On June 18, 2025, the IRS posted an administrative clarification on its About Form 6765 webpage addressing the January 2025 Form 6765 instructions regarding qualified research expenses (QREs) and controlled group reporting rules.

In News Release IR-2025-99 (October 1, 2025), the IRS extended the public feedback and comment period on the draft Form 6765 instructions through March 31, 2026, and confirmed that Section G would remain optional for all filers for tax year 2025 (tax years beginning before January 1, 2026). That comment period closed on March 31, 2026.

The current official Instructions for Form 6765 bear the IRS revision designation "Rev. December 2025" (with tax accounting firms reporting public posting on irs.gov in early February 2026, specifically February 5–6, 2026). This report cites the official IRS revision label ("Rev. December 2025" / "Rev. 12/2025").

In addition to Section G, the redesigned Form 6765 (effective beginning with tax year 2024 filings) added new mandatory header and Section E questions requiring taxpayers to disclose: (1) the total number of business components generating QREs (Line 37); (2) the exact amount of officer wages included in total QREs (Line 38); (3) whether the taxpayer acquired or disposed of any major trade or business during the tax year under IRC § 41(f)(3) (Line 39); (4) whether the taxpayer identified any new categories of expenditures included as QREs compared to prior years (Line 40); and (5) whether any portion of the QREs was determined using the ASC 730 Directive or statistical sampling (Line 41).

body.text: 5.2 Section G: When It Is Required

Under News Release IR-2025-99 and the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025), completion of Section G (Business Component Information) is optional for all filers for tax years beginning before January 1, 2026 (including the 2024 and 2025 tax years), and becomes mandatory for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025 (starting with 2026 tax year returns). Once Section G is generally mandatory, a taxpayer is exempt from completing Section G only if it satisfies either of the following two specific exceptions:

items: Qualified Small Business Payroll Tax Credit Exception: The taxpayer is a Qualified Small Business (QSB), as defined under IRC § 41(h)(3), that checks the applicable box on Form 6765 to elect the reduced payroll tax credit under IRC § 41(h)(1) and (2); or

Small Taxpayer Original-Return Exception: The taxpayer has total qualified research expenses (QREs) of $1.5 million or less, determined at the controlled group level, and has equal to or less than $50 million of gross receipts, as determined under IRC § 448(c)(3) (without regard to subparagraph (A) thereof; described in the instructions as average annual gross receipts for the three prior tax years), and the taxpayer is claiming the research credit on an original filed return.

(a) Statutory Citation for QSB Definition: While paragraphs (1) and (2) of IRC § 41(h) govern the mechanics and annual limitations of the payroll tax credit election, the statutory definition of a "qualified small business" (requiring gross receipts of less than $5 million for the taxable year and no gross receipts for any taxable year preceding the 5-taxable-year period ending with such taxable year) is codified in IRC § 41(h)(3), as explicitly cited in IR-2025-99 and the Form 6765 Instructions.

(b) Omission of the Original-Return Condition: That restriction has a major operational impact on R&D tax refund claims: if a taxpayer with $1.5 million or less in QREs and $50 million or less in gross receipts fails to claim the credit on its original 2026 return and subsequently files an amended return (refund claim) for the 2026 tax year, the small-taxpayer exemption is unavailable, and the taxpayer must complete Section G in full on the amended return.

body.text: 5.3 Section G: Column Structure and the 80% / Top-50 Business Component Rule

For taxpayers required to complete Section G (for tax years beginning after December 31, 2025), the Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) require reporting of business components in descending order of QRE amount until the listed business components account for at least 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components directly itemized, with any remaining business components aggregated into a single row labeled "Aggregate/All Other." (If a taxpayer utilizes a valid statistical sample under Rev. Proc. 2011-42, it must report 100% of the business components in the sample up to the top 50, and aggregate the remainder.)
The verified column structure under the December 2025 Instructions is set forth below:

headers: Content Required (Instructions for Form 6765, Rev. December 2025)

cells: Employer Identification Number (EIN) of the controlled group member or entity conducting the research activities
Principal Business Activity (PBA) code of the entity
Business component name or unique alphanumeric identifier, which must be consistent with the taxpayer's books and records
Business component type: select Product, Process, or All Others (which includes computer software, technique, formula, or invention)

Software classification (completed only if the business component involves software): Internal Use Software (IUS), Dual Function Software (DFS), Non-IUS (commercial software held for sale, lease, or license), or Excepted from IUS treatment

Information sought to be discovered (Amended returns only): describes the technological information sought to be discovered to overcome uncertainty; required when claiming a refund or credit on an amended return, and not required on timely filed original returns (including extensions)
Qualified in-house wages of employees directly conducting/performing the qualified research
Qualified in-house wages of first-line managers and supervisors directly supervising the qualified research
Qualified in-house wages of employees directly supporting the qualified research
Total qualified wages for the business component (sum of Columns 50, 51, and 52; total across Section G carries to Line 42)
Qualified supplies used in the conduct of qualified research for the business component (carries to Line 43)
Qualified rental or lease costs of off-premises computers (cloud computing/hosting costs used in qualified research; carries to Line 44)
Applicable percentage of qualified contract research expenses for the business component (carries to Line 45)

body.text: As reflected in Column 49(f) of the table above and confirmed by the December 2025 Form 6765 Instructions, describing the "information sought to be discovered" at the business-component level in Column 49(f) is required only when the research credit is claimed on an amended return (or AAR), and may be left blank on a timely filed original return (including extensions). Note that Column 49(f) requires the information sought to be discovered for the business component, which aligns with the post-FAQ 21 standard and does not reinstate the waived requirement to provide individual-by-individual narratives at filing.
5.4 Amended-Return Rules in the Instructions
The Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) and related administrative guidance establish strict procedural rules for amended-return refund claims:

items: Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) Election under IRC § 41(c)(4): Pursuant to Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(2) and the Form 6765 Instructions, a taxpayer may make an election to compute the research credit using the Alternative Simplified Credit (ASC) method on an amended return for a tax year only if the taxpayer has not previously claimed the Section 41 credit (under the regular credit method) for that tax year on an original or previously filed amended return. Once a taxpayer claims the regular credit on an original or amended return, it may not switch to the ASC method on a subsequent amended return for that year.

Controlled Group Conformity for ASC Elections: Within a controlled group of corporations or businesses under common control (IRC § 41(f)(1)), a member may not make an ASC election on an amended return for a tax year if any member of the controlled group previously claimed the research credit for that tax year using the regular credit method on an original or amended return. That phrasing does not appear in the Form 6765 Instructions; rather, Treas. Reg. § 1.41-9(b)(2) and the instructions prohibit making an amended-return ASC election if any group member already claimed the credit under the regular method for that tax year, and provide that the designated member's election (or revocation) on a timely original return binds all members of the controlled group.

IRC § 280C(c) Reduced Credit Election: Under IRC § 280C(c)(2) (redesignated as IRC § 280C(c)(2) following P.L. 119-21; formerly § 280C(c)(3)), the election to claim a reduced research credit (reducing the credit by the maximum corporate tax rate of 21%, yielding a net credit equal to 79% of the gross credit in lieu of reducing the IRC § 174 / § 174A deduction) must be made on Item A of Form 6765 on a timely filed original return (including extensions) and is irrevocable for that tax year. It cannot be made or revoked on an amended return. A narrow statutory transition exception enacted under § 70302(f) of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (P.L. 119-21) and implemented in Section 6 of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 permitted eligible small business taxpayers (meeting the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test) that elected retroactive Section 174A expensing for tax years 2022–2024 to make a late § 280C(c) election—or revoke a prior § 280C(c) election—on an amended return or AAR filed on or before the earlier of July 6, 2026, or the IRC § 6511 refund statute of limitations date.

Mandatory Binary Attachment Filenames for Electronic Filing (E-File): To facilitate automated processing of electronic original and amended returns, the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765 mandate exact PDF attachment filenames depending on the disclosure:
Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf (statement detailing reduced IRC § 174 / § 174A deductions or capitalized expenditures when the Item A § 280C(c) election is not made);
Form6765ItemBGroupCredit.pdf (statement detailing controlled group member QRE and credit allocation under Item B);

Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf (statement providing the mandatory three items of refund-claim validity information—and Column 49(f) details where Section G is not completed—when claiming a refund on an amended return);
Form6765Study.pdf (optional or supplemental R&D credit study attached to an amended return); and
Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf (statistical sampling plan attached when Line 41 indicates the use of statistical sampling under Rev. Proc. 2011-42).

No Safe Harbor from Statistical Sampling Acceptance: The Form 6765 Instructions explicitly state that the IRS's processing of a filed Form 6765 or acceptance of an attached Form6765StatSamplePlan.pdf does not constitute acceptance by the IRS that the taxpayer's statistical sample complies with Rev. Proc. 2011-42 or serves as adequate substantiation upon audit.

body.text: 6. Section 174A as It Affects Form 6765 and Refund Claims

To maintain strict scope lock, this section addresses only the statutory rules under new IRC § 174A, the conforming amendment to IRC § 280C(c)(1), and the procedural rules in Rev. Proc. 2025-28 that directly govern Form 6765 reporting and amended-return refund claims.

items: Enactment of IRC § 174A(a) (Immediate Domestic Expensing): Section 70302 of P.L. 119-21 added IRC § 174A to the Internal Revenue Code. Under IRC § 174A(a), taxpayers may immediately deduct domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2024, permanently reversing the mandatory five-year domestic amortization rule that had applied since 2022 under the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (P.L. 115-97). Foreign research or experimental expenditures remain subject to mandatory 15-year amortization under IRC § 174(a)–(b).

Elective Amortization under IRC § 174A(c): Alternatively, under IRC § 174A(c), a taxpayer may elect to capitalize and ratably amortize domestic research or experimental expenditures over a period of not less than 60 months, beginning with the month in which the taxpayer first realizes benefits from such expenditures.

Interaction with the Research Credit under IRC § 280C(c)(1): P.L. 119-21 amended IRC § 280C(c)(1) to restore the classic pre-2022 coordination rule for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 (and for retroactive small-business election years). Specifically, a taxpayer that does not make the IRC § 280C(c)(2) reduced credit election on Item A of Form 6765 must reduce its otherwise allowable domestic research deduction under IRC § 174A(a)—or the amount chargeable to capital account under IRC § 174(a) or § 174A(c)—by 100% of the amount of the gross Section 41 research credit claimed. Pursuant to the Form 6765 Instructions and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 § 2.05(2), the taxpayer must attach a statement (Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf) reporting the exact deduction or capitalized expenditure amounts reduced by the credit. Under the amended text of IRC § 280C(c)(1), the statute directly coordinates the reduction across both current deductions under § 174A(a) and amounts chargeable to capital account for capitalized research expenditures.

Transition Recovery Rules under OBBBA § 70302(f) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28: For domestic research or experimental expenditures paid or incurred in taxable years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025 (generally the 2022, 2023, and 2024 tax years) that were capitalized and amortized under former IRC § 174, OBBBA § 70302(f)(2) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 permit all taxpayers to elect to accelerate recovery of the remaining unamortized balance either: (1) in full as a deduction in the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (the 2025 tax year); or (2) ratably over the two-taxable-year period beginning with the first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024 (50% in 2025 and 50% in 2026). Under Rev. Proc. 2025-28, this recovery is implemented as an automatic change in method of accounting under IRC § 446(e) applied on a cut-off basis, with no IRC § 481(a) adjustment. (Subsequent guidance in Rev. Proc. 2026-32 extended the waiver of certain automatic method-change eligibility restrictions through tax years beginning before January 1, 2028.)

Continuing the Prior Five-Year Amortization Schedule: Because accelerating unamortized 2022–2024 domestic expenditures under OBBBA § 70302(f)(2) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28 is structured as an affirmative election, a taxpayer that does not make the acceleration election (and does not make the small-business retroactive expensing election) continues to amortize those pre-2025 domestic balances over the remainder of their original five-year IRC § 174 amortization schedule.
Retroactive Small-Business Refund Claims and Procedural Cut-Off Dates: In Rev. Proc. 2025-28:

For a taxpayer's 2024 tax year return filed on or before November 15, 2025 (or before the release of Rev. Proc. 2025-28 on August 28, 2025), special transition deemed-election and superseding-return rules applied; under Section 7.02(3)(c), an eligible small business filing an original pre-2025 return after August 28, 2025, could apply the retroactive IRC § 174A expensing method directly by attaching the required election statement.

To qualify as an "eligible taxpayer" (small business) entitled under OBBBA § 70302(f)(1) to file amended returns (or AARs) applying IRC § 174A immediate expensing retroactively to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, and before January 1, 2025 (2022–2024), the taxpayer had to satisfy the IRC § 448(c) gross receipts test for its first taxable year beginning after December 31, 2024—meaning average annual gross receipts for the three preceding tax years of $31,000,000 or less (the inflation-adjusted § 448(c) threshold for 2025 under Rev. Proc. 2024-40) and could not be a tax shelter under IRC § 448(d)(3).

Under OBBBA § 70302(f)(1)(C) and Rev. Proc. 2025-28, all amended returns or AARs making the small-business retroactive IRC § 174A election—along with any accompanying late IRC § 280C(c) elections or revocations—had to be filed on or before the earlier of July 6, 2026 (one year after enactment of P.L. 119-21, adjusted for the weekend/holiday rule under IRC § 7503) or the expiration of the IRC § 6511 statute of limitations for credit or refund for the relevant tax year (which, for calendar-year 2022 returns filed on April 15, 2023, without extension, expired earlier on April 15, 2026). As of November 11, 2026, the July 6, 2026 statutory window for retroactive Section 174A small-business amended returns has closed. Crucially, however, the closure of the July 6, 2026 Section 174A election window does not curtail the regular three-year statute of limitations under IRC § 6511(a) for filing a standalone Section 41 research credit refund claim for otherwise open tax years (such as 2023, 2024, or 2025), nor does a pure Section 174A deduction change (that does not claim or increase a Section 41 credit) trigger the three-item Section 41 refund claim validity screening rules.

body.text: 7. The Examination Stage

Passing the IRS's initial three-item administrative validity screening (or curing a deficiency within the 45-day perfection period through January 10, 2027) merely admits the refund claim for substantive processing; it does not insulate the claim from examination. When a research credit refund claim is selected for audit by the IRS Large Business and International (LB&I) or Small Business/Self-Employed (SB/SE) divisions, examiners are expressly authorized under FAQ 21 to request the individual-level documentation waived at filing (the names of the individuals who performed each research activity and the specific technological information each individual sought to discover), and the claim is evaluated under federal judicial standards of proof.

items: General Burden of Proof: In U.S. Tax Court and federal refund litigation involving the IRC § 41 research credit, tax credits are a matter of legislative grace, and the taxpayer bears the burden of proving both that its activities satisfy every element of the four-part statutory test under IRC § 41(d) for each business component and the exact amount of its qualified research expenses (Kapur v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-28, citing INDOPCO, Inc. v. Commissioner, 503 U.S. 79, 84 (1992), and Feigh v. Commissioner, 152 T.C. 267 (2019); Tax Court Rule 142(a)).

Role of Credible Testimony and Reasonable Estimates (Suder v. Commissioner): Under Treasury Regulation § 1.41-4(d) (T.D. 9104), a taxpayer is not required to keep records in a particular manner, provided that the records maintained are in sufficiently usable form and detail to substantiate that the expenditures claimed are eligible for the credit. In Suder v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2014-201 (filed October 1, 2014), the Tax Court evaluated wage QRE allocations for Eric Suder, the chief executive officer of Estech Systems, Inc. (ESI), for tax years 2004 through 2007. ESI's senior vice president of product development, Robert Wende, testified and estimated that 75% of Mr. Suder's time was devoted to qualified research services across multiple telephone system business components. The Tax Court found Mr. Wende's testimony highly credible and accepted his 75% allocation as a reasonable estimate because it was extensively corroborated by contemporaneous documentary evidence (including emails, design notes, patent applications, and product specifications) as well as the testimony of other witnesses. Review of T.C. Memo. 2014-201 confirms that the percentage allocations were established primarily by Mr. Wende, the senior vice president of product development who worked closely with Mr. Suder on a daily basis, corroborated by other company personnel and contemporaneous project records.

Judicial Limits on Oral Testimony and the Cohan Rule (Little Sandy Coal and Shami): Federal courts strictly limit the use of the Cohan estimation rule (Cohan v. Commissioner, 39 F.2d 540 (2d Cir. 1930)) in Section 41 research credit disputes. Under established precedent—including United States v. McFerrin, 570 F.3d 672 (5th Cir. 2009), and Shami v. Commissioner, 741 F.3d 560 (5th Cir. 2014)—a court will not estimate the amount of qualified wages for an employee unless the taxpayer first establishes with credible evidence that the specific employee actually performed qualified services on a qualified business component, and provides a satisfactory evidentiary basis for making a rational estimate. Furthermore, in Little Sandy Coal Co., Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), both the Tax Court and the Seventh Circuit held that generalized oral testimony and arbitrary percentage estimates, unsupported by time records or project-level documentation tracking employee hours between experimental and non-experimental activities, were legally insufficient to prove that "substantially all" (at least 80% under Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(a)(6)) of the taxpayer's research activities constituted elements of a process of experimentation for the business components at issue. Thus, while reasonable estimates corroborated by documentation may sometimes substantiate the amount of QREs once qualification is proven, uncorroborated estimates cannot establish foundational eligibility under the four-part test or the "substantially all" threshold.

Conditions for Shifting the Burden of Proof under IRC § 7491(a): Under IRC § 7491(a)(1), if a taxpayer introduces credible evidence with respect to any factual issue relevant to ascertaining the taxpayer's tax liability in a court proceeding, the burden of proof shifts to the Secretary only as to that specific factual issue, and only if the taxpayer satisfies all three mandatory threshold conditions set forth in IRC § 7491(a)(2): Because the vast majority of corporate R&D tax refund disputes turn on failure to maintain adequate substantiation or involve entities exceeding the $7 million net worth cap, the burden of proof rarely shifts under IRC § 7491(a) in research credit cases, and there is no concept of a "mathematical" burden shift in the statute or case law.
The taxpayer has complied with all requirements under the Internal Revenue Code to substantiate any item (IRC § 7491(a)(2)(A));

The taxpayer has maintained all records required under the Internal Revenue Code and has cooperated with reasonable requests by the Secretary for witnesses, information, documents, meetings, and interviews (IRC § 7491(a)(2)(B)); and

In the case of a partnership, corporation, or trust, the taxpayer meets the net worth and size limitations of IRC § 7430(c)(4)(A)(ii) (referencing 28 U.S.C. § 2412(d)(2)(B)), which requires that the entity's net worth did not exceed $7,000,000 and that it did not have more than 500 employees at the time the litigation was commenced (IRC § 7491(a)(2)(C)).

body.text: 8. Analysis: What the Current Guidance Means for Refund Claims
This section synthesizes the practical compliance implications of the verified authorities for taxpayers preparing Section 41 refund claims.

items: Substantive Preparation Remains Unchanged Despite the FAQ 21 Filing Waiver: Although FAQ 21 lowered the administrative threshold for what must be physically attached to an amended return at filing (requiring three items rather than five), it did not reduce the substantive evidentiary burden upon audit. Because the IRS explicitly reserves the right to request employee names and the specific information each individual sought to discover during an examination—and because Section G of Form 6765 requires Column 49(f) ("information sought to be discovered" at the business-component level) on amended returns along with wages broken down by direct conduct (Column 50), direct supervision (Column 51), and direct support (Column 52)—taxpayers must still compile full employee-by-component and activity-level substantiation contemporaneously before filing a refund claim.

Convergence of Section G and Refund-Claim Validity Rules for 2026 and Later Tax Years: For tax years beginning after December 31, 2025, the mandatory Section G disclosures on Form 6765 overlap substantially with the three items of information required for a valid refund claim. Critically, because the small-taxpayer exemption from Section G ($1.5 million or less in QREs and $50 million or less in gross receipts) is conditioned on claiming the credit on an original return, a smaller taxpayer that omits the R&D credit on its original 2026 return and later files an amended return to claim a refund forfeits that exemption and must complete Section G—including Column 49(f)—in addition to satisfying the refund claim validity requirements.

Imminent Expiration of the 45-Day Perfection Period on January 10, 2027: With the transition period scheduled to end on January 10, 2027, under IR-2025-99, the 45-day cure window (via Letter 6426C or Letter 6428) cannot be relied upon for claims filed after that date unless the IRS announces a further extension. If a refund claim is filed near the expiration of the three-year IRC § 6511 statute of limitations after January 10, 2027, and is rejected as deficient without a perfection window, the taxpayer may lose the ability to refile a corrected claim before the statute of limitations closes.

body.text: Hypothetical Example (Illustrative Only)

Consider a hypothetical C corporation (not a member of a controlled group) that incurs $1.2 million of qualified research expenses (QREs) and has $40 million of average annual gross receipts (determined under IRC § 448(c)(3) for the three prior tax years) for its calendar tax year 2026. The corporation is not a Qualified Small Business electing the IRC § 41(h) payroll tax credit.

items: Scenario A — Claimed on a Timely Original 2026 Return: Because the taxpayer's QREs ($1.2 million) are equal to or less than $1.5 million, its average annual gross receipts ($40 million) are equal to or less than $50 million, and it claims the research credit on a timely filed original return, it qualifies for the small-taxpayer exception under the December 2025 Instructions for Form 6765. Consequently, Section G of Form 6765 is optional, and Column 49(f) is not required.

Scenario B — Claimed Later on an Amended 2026 Return (Refund Claim): Suppose the same corporation does not claim the research credit on its original 2026 Form 1120 and subsequently files Form 1120-X in 2027 to claim a Section 41 refund for the 2026 tax year. Because the credit is not claimed on an original return, the small-taxpayer exemption from Section G does not apply. Under the current Instructions for Form 6765 (Rev. December 2025) and the IRS refund-claim validity rules, the taxpayer must: (1) complete Section G of Form 6765 in full, including Column 49(f) detailing the information sought to be discovered for each reported business component; (2) satisfy all three mandatory refund-claim validity items (identifying all business components, all research activities performed for each component, and total wage, supply, and contract research QREs, attached as Form6765ClaimInformation.pdf if e-filed); and (3) reduce its 2026 IRC § 174A domestic research deduction by 100% of the claimed gross credit on the amended return (attaching Form6765ItemASection280C.pdf), because the IRC § 280C(c) reduced credit election could only have been made on the original timely filed return.
